text:
Bean, Runner.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Runner beans make a colourful screen as well as a crop. Red, white or pink flowers give way to long flat pods. The plants need more moisture than French beans, especially when the pods set. Pick young pods every few days. Older stringed varieties need a little more preparation in the kitchen.

Quick facts
Sow

Outdoors late May in the south, early Jun in colder gardens.

Harvest

Jul – Sep

Germination

7–14 days

Sowing depth

2 in.

Row spacing

18 in. between rows

Plant spacing

9 in. between plants

Ready in

About 12–14 weeks from sowing

Sow indoors

Apr in pots for an early start.

Plant out

Late May–early Jun after frost.

Recommended varieties
STICK RUNNER BEANS
Moonlight

White-flowered runner–French cross with reliable pod set and tender green pods.

STICK RUNNER BEANS
Firestorm

Red-flowered runner–French cross for reliable cropping on a bean frame.

STICK RUNNER BEANS
Enorma

Traditional long-podded runner for tall supports; long, straight beans.

STICK RUNNER BEANS
White Lady

White-flowered climber with long, tender pods. Pick young and often.

DWARF RUNNER BEANS
Pickwick

Dwarf runner for containers and small plots, with less yield than a full-height frame.

Key risks
No pods

Runner beans often fail to set pods when roots become dry, when weather is very hot and dry, or when pollinating insects are scarce.

Halo blight

Semi-transparent or water-soaked spots with yellow halos on leaves are a warning sign.

Black bean aphid

Black aphids can gather on soft runner-bean growth, leaving sticky honeydew and distorted leaves.

Slugs

Slugs are the chief pest of young runner bean plants, especially in cool, wet weather while growth is slow.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
22
PEAS & BEANS

Rich soil and shelter.

Choose a sunny site with moist, free-draining ground.

Pinch out at support height.

Remove growing points once plants reach the tops of their supports.

Keep roots steadily moist.

Water thoroughly from flowering onwards for a good pod set.

Soil & preparation
Use sunny, sheltered, rich ground that holds moisture but drains well. Lime acid soil if needed towards pH 6.5.
Prepare deeply with compost or well-rotted manure in autumn or winter. Avoid shading neighbouring crops.
Sowing & planting
Set sturdy supports
Sow beside the poles
Establish the double row
Set the poles 

Tie crossed poles to a horizontal top cane, or make a wigwam for a smaller bed.

Sow 

In warm soil, sow at the base of each pole, 2 in. deep. Sow a few spare seeds at the row ends.

Plant out 

For an early crop, raise plants singly in pots. Harden them off and set one beside each support once frost risk has passed.

Looking after the crop
Guard against slugs, tie young stems loosely and hoe. Mulch strong-growing plants, especially on light soil or in dry gardens.
Water deeply from flowering in dry weather. Steady moisture helps pods set.
Use organic liquid feed if growth weakens or plants carry a heavy crop. Pinch growing points at the tops of supports.
After frost, remove supports and compost stems. Leave roots and stem bases where practical; mulch for the next crop.
Harvesting & storage
Pick flat, tender pods about 6–8 in. long, before beans swell. Hold the vine in one hand; snap pods off with the other to avoid tearing stems.
Pick every couple of days while the crop lasts. Pods left to ripen slow further production.
Mature pods only for drying or seed. White-bean types such as Czar can crop in autumn; dry pods thoroughly before shelling and storing.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
No pods	Flowers drop; few pods set.	Mulch and water well from flowering.
Halo blight	Wet spots with yellow halos.	Remove sick plants; save no seed; rotate.
Black bean aphid	Black colonies; curled growth.	Squash colonies; encourage predators.
Slugs	Chewed young plants.	Plant in warm soil; hand-pick slugs.
Mosaic disease	Mottled, distorted leaves.	Remove affected plants; use healthy seed.
Birds and animals	Seeds or seedlings disappear.	Raise in modules; protect with secure netting.
Bean disease	Dark, red-edged pod spots.	Remove sick plants; save no seed; rotate.
Bean seed fly	Tunnelled, failing seedlings.	Remove damaged plants; start beans in modules.
Final tips

Soak seed only if halo blight has not been a problem.

A warm July sowing may crop in autumn if soil stays moist.

Keep roots moist from flowering.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 100–103
